title: Age differences, age changes, and generalizability in marathon running by master athletes
population: World Top 100 age-class marathon performances (937 performances by 387 men, 856 by 301 women), mean ages 62.05 and 60.5
findings: Critiques the paradigm that age-class record lists are a 'virtual' cross-sectional study of aging; best-fitting mixed model on log performance time includes linear and quadratic terms for entry cohort age and elapsed age.
Rates of increase in performance time are higher at older cohort ages and elapsed ages, with greater increases in women than men.

Increases in performance time with cohort age and elapsed age are higher in slower than faster performance quartiles; faster-quartile athletes more likely have multiple entries and slower-quartile athletes single entries.
The author evaluates generalizability from the fastest quartile to slower quartiles.
limitations: Elite-level archival top-100 lists; selection effects; log-time model; no training data. The abstract does not mention WMA age-grading tables, so the link to them is the verifier's inference.
implications: Do not assume record-list age curves (the basis of WMA-style age grading) describe typical recreational runners; this paper suggests slower athletes decline faster than the fastest quartile.
Where age grading is shown, label it as a rough comparison to elite standards and prefer the athlete's own longitudinal trend for target setting.
Allow faster decline slopes for slower or less consistent runners than elite-derived curves; the data cannot give a number.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC abstract match. Sample size 688 = 387 + 301 athletes (stated in abstract). No validation paper for WMA factors was found by researcher or verifier.
